About me

Physicist who builds the tools as well as the chips

I grew up in Pakistan and came to Berlin for physics, where I completed both my bachelor’s and my master’s at TU Berlin with a grade of 1.3. Since 2024 I have worked in the Hybrid PICs group at Fraunhofer HHI, designing polymer and silicon nitride components, taking them to tape-out and measuring quantum light in the lab, while my master’s thesis took me deep into numerical methods for open quantum systems.

How I work

Independent, and ahead of deadlines.Finishing early leaves room to go further on a component, into directions nobody had planned to explore.
I look for where an approach breaks.Approximations have limits. I check the conditions under which a method stops holding, so problems don’t come back later in fabrication or in the lab.
I fix what limits the setup.On our photon-pair setup I traced the weak points and added live wavelength tracking, photon-based fibre alignment through a Moku signal chain, and pump power stabilisation, which made the measurements more reliable.
I turn each project into reusable tools.Two AWG design packages, measurement scripts with live plotting and HDF5 storage, an MMI optimiser: tools nobody asked for, that colleagues appreciate. Each project also teaches me a better way to do the next one.

Outside the lab

  • Music. I play piano and guitar.
  • Reading. Novels from both Western and Japanese writers.
  • Languages. I taught myself Japanese, far enough to follow conversations and read simple kanji.
  • Long walks, the best place to think a problem through.
  • Coffee. I worked as a barista, so cappuccino, latte, Milchkaffee or cortado: I make a serious cup.

The work in detail

Real design files, raw lab data and live simulations, running in your browser. Jump to photonics, the lab or theory.

Fraunhofer HHIHybrid PICs groupJune 2024 – present

Photonic integrated circuits

I design passive components on polymer and silicon nitride platforms, from mode solving to GDSII mask. Every design I list here went into a fabrication run, and each one carries a tolerance analysis against realistic fabrication variance, using Ansys optiSLang and manual parameter sweeps to find optima that survive the fab.

Arrayed waveguide gratings

Four polymer AWG variants, 8 and 16 channels at 1550 nm, designed in both Lumerical and Luceda IPKISS. They separate SPDC photon pairs inside a PolyBoard system with −30 dB crosstalk.

MMI couplers and splitters

Five MMIs on silicon nitride (1×2, 1×3, 3×3, 4×4 and a 9×9 Talbot-effect splitter that distributes light for optical machine-learning training) and two on polymer.

785 nm PolyBoard chip

A full chip architecture in the visible range: fibre-to-chip interface, thin-film filters, tap coupler and MMI, with radial profiling to find the minimum bend radius of the polymer waveguides.

Thin-film filters

Geometric parametrisation across RGB, infrared and 1550 nm bands for polarising beam splitters, dichroic mirrors and bandpass filters.

In pair mode a 775 nm pump splits into signal and idler photons whose energies add up to the pump photon (1/λs + 1/λi = 1/775 nm), so they sit on either side of 1550 nm and land in mirrored ports. That is how my AWGs split SPDC photon pairs. The test-laser mode shows what a single C-band probe would see.

Thin-film-filter polarisation combiner at 1550 nm

Real design data

Two polymer waveguides carry TE and TM light into a multilayer dielectric filter set at 45° in a glue-filled trench. One polarisation passes through the filter, the other is reflected, and both leave through a shared output waveguide. I built the 3D FDTD model to analyse the combiner's dispersion across the band and to check how it tolerates fabrication errors; those tolerance results set the waveguide offsets around the filter in the fabricated device. Drawn to scale from that model's geometry; select a part to see its role.

Lumerical Python AWG PDK

Written from scratch: free propagation regions, array waveguides, design rules and the AWG calculation method, through simulation to GDSII mask generation.

Luceda IPKISS AWG package

A surrogate PDK with a custom material platform, built on IPKISS base functions. I added a router for arbitrary fixed-bend waveguides, because IPKISS only offered U- and S-bends.

Design rules both packages enforce
  • Minimum spacing between array waveguides
  • Smooth taper between free propagation region and array
  • Minimum resolvable feature size
  • No waveguide crossings
  • Minimum bend radius
Also in the simulation toolbox
  • Automated N×N MMI optimisation with optiSLang and 3D FDTD, verified by EME, geometry read from the GDS layout (in progress, first stage live below)
  • Single-mode and adiabatic taper simulations
  • Mode coupling of Bragg reflection waveguides to pick the best fibre interface
  • SPAD photon-production curves versus source angle in Lumerical FDTD

Both packages are on GitHub

Robust N×N MMI optimiser

In development

The fast first stage of my MMI optimisation pipeline, running live. A finite-difference solver finds every guided mode of the MMI, each access port is projected onto them, and the transfer matrix follows from mode propagation. A design is scored on its worst case over three wavelengths (1530, 1550, 1570 nm) and three fabrication width biases (−0.3, 0, +0.3 µm), with penalties for lithography limits and footprint.

Design and score
Robust cost map: length × pitch

Uses the placeholder indices from my code (core 1.56, cladding 1.53, 3.2 µm thick core, TE), not platform material data. Length and pitch are scaled to the self-imaging theory for the current width, so the search space stays well conditioned when the width changes. The browser port reproduces the Python model to every printed digit. Stages 2–4 are written and so far tested against mock solvers. The optimiser is still in development and not yet on GitHub.

Quantum light in the lab

I characterise nonlinear photon-pair sources for quantum key distribution: periodically poled lithium niobate (PPLN) crystals and Bragg reflection waveguides (BRW). I measure phase-matching temperatures, wavelength tuning curves and SPDC pair peaks, and run the inverse process, second-harmonic generation, to check coupling and efficiency. The setup uses single-photon counters, a time tagger and a tunable diode laser, and I adapt it per project with custom splitters and pump-suppression filters.

Sweep · click a point to open its histogram
Time-tagger histogram

Every point is a raw two-detector time-tagger histogram, acquired for 1 minute with 1 ns bins at 0.5 mW pump power. I count pairs in the 2 ns window around the coincidence peak and subtract the accidental background, taken as the median of the flat region beyond 60 ns; CAR is net pairs divided by accidentals in the same window. Pair generation switches on sharply at 779.2 nm, peaks near 781 nm and falls off towards longer pump wavelengths, while the temperature sweep stays broad with CAR 26–30 throughout.

How CAR scales with pump power

Model
Coincidence-to-accidental ratio —Measured: PPLN ≈ 29 at 0.5 mW; BRW module ≈ 15 at 3 mW

Pairs grow linearly with pump power, while accidental coincidences between unrelated photons grow quadratically, so CAR falls as you pump harder. Each model curve is calibrated to my measurements: the PPLN crystal at 0.5 mW and the packaged BRW module at 3 mW. The histogram adds counting noise. The BRW values use a 5 ns window and the PPLN value a 2 ns window, so compare the trends rather than the absolute numbers.

BRW photon-pair source, from bare chip to packaged module

Raw lab data

The same chip measured at every packaging stage: the bare waveguide, the sub-assembly, and the fibre-coupled module with an MMI, a pump filter and two optical isolators. Pick a stage to see its pump-wavelength sweep and the raw time-tagger histograms behind it.

Pump-wavelength sweep · click a point
Time-tagger histogram

1-minute acquisitions per point at 3 mW pump power. Pairs are counted in a 5 ns window around each setup's coincidence peak (the module shows two peaks 2 ns apart), minus the accidental background from the flat region more than 40 ns away; CAR is net pairs over accidentals in that window. The wider window suits every stage alike, so CAR values here are conservative. In the packaged module, the filter and two isolators keep the background low enough for a CAR of up to 30.

Choosing the fibre for a Bragg reflection waveguide

Real design data

The BRW source is pumped at 775 nm in a Bragg mode that is wide and flat, so no round fibre mode matches it perfectly. I solved the mode of the etched ridge in Lumerical and computed its overlap with Gaussian fibre modes to decide which fibre to couple with. Here the overlap is recomputed live from the exported mode field, so you can also test misalignment.

Coupling into the BRW mode—
For comparison, centred—Standard PM780-HP fibre, MFD 5.3 µm
BRW mode at 775 nm with fibre mode outline
Overlap against fibre MFD
Alignment tolerance at this MFD

Overlap η = |∫EBRW Efibre dA|² / (∫|EBRW|² dA ∫|Efibre|² dA) on the solver's non-uniform mesh, with a Gaussian fibre field exp(−r²/w₀²), w₀ = MFD/2. Dots are my Lumerical overlap results; the live calculation matches them within 0.002 from 1.5 µm upward. The optimum near 2.5 µm is why I couple this chip with a lensed fibre of 2.5 µm spot size rather than a cleaved fibre.

Aligning fibres with the photons themselves

Fibre-to-waveguide alignment usually relies on visible light. I built a signal chain that turns single-photon detector pulses into a steady voltage, so an automatic alignment tool can optimise coupling on the SPDC photons directly. It is the alignment loop in the setup diagram above.

Open quantum many-body dynamics

Real quantum systems leak into their environment, and that environment remembers. I developed a local expansion for second-order non-Markovian quantum state diffusion that avoids diagonalising the Hamiltonian. It gives a positivity-preserving unravelling, equivalent to the Redfield equation at second order, that scales to many-body lattices when combined with matrix product states.

Disordered XXZ spin chains with up to 35 sites, run as parallel stochastic trajectories on up to ≈52 GPUs of the TU Berlin mathematics cluster.

Correlated-noise generator for an Ohmic bath

Port of my Julia code

The bath has spectral density J(ω) = γ ω e−ω/ωc at temperature T, so its correlation function α(t) = ∫ J(ω) [(n(ω)+1) e−iωt + n(ω) eiωt] dω is complex. The generator builds a kernel R(t) with α = R ⋆ R* from √S(ω), the square root of the FFT of α, and convolves it with complex white noise. Change the bath and the check reruns 2000 realisations in your browser.

One noise realisation z(t)
⟨z(t) z*(s)⟩ against the target α(t − s), s = 4

Same parameters as my thesis script: γ = 0.06, time step 0.05, memory support of 5 time units before t = 0. In the thesis these trajectories drive the non-Markovian quantum state diffusion equation; the fine-grid noise is averaged onto the integrator's coarse time step with Simpson's rule and checked against the downsampled Toeplitz correlation matrix. Units are dimensionless with ℏ = kB = 1.

Code

Extended ITensors.jl with my own backend for the stochastic dissipator and the nonlinear stochastic differential equation solver, using MPS/MPO and TDVP. The noise generator and correlation calculator are fully self-written.

Verification

Convergence in the hard low-temperature regime, benchmarked against the Redfield equation. The physics studied: entanglement growth and energy transport.

Where it leads

Correlated, non-Markovian noise is what real qubits see. Next, I plan a public surface-code memory study under correlated noise with Stim and PyMatching, reusing this generator.

Publication · first author · preprint forthcoming November 2026 Local unraveling of dissipative quantum many-body dynamics beyond ultra-weak coupling A. Wasay, A. Schnell, A. Eckardt, V. Link
